# Exercise 1

The Week 3.1 R lecture companion shows examples how to test the hypothesis 
phyp = 0.5 and how to find approximately a 95% confidence interval, using the
number of successes in a sample of size n = 10 selected from a binomial 
distribution with probability of success p = 0.2.

Modify the code to investigate the following questions and write down your 
conclusions. You should make several runs with independently selected samples 
to ensure that your conclusions are reliable.

1. For hypothesis testing with fixed phyp = 0.5 and p = 0.2, how do the changes of n
affect the results?
2. For hypothesis testing with fixed phyp = 0.5 and n = 10, how do the changes of p
affect the results? Answer this question also for n = 5, n = 100 and n = 1000.
3. For hypothesis testing with fixed p = 0.2 and n = 10, how do the changes of phyp
affect the results? Answer this question also for n = 5, n = 100 and n = 1000.
4. (optional) Answer the first two questions for a one-tailed hypothesis. Answer the
third question for “equally spread” deviations.
5. For confidence intervals with fixed confidence level 1 − α = 95% and p = 0.2, how
do the changes of n affect the results? Use any form of a confidence interval you
find convenient.
6. For confidence intervals with fixed n = 10 and p = 0.2, how do the changes of
the confidence level 1 − α affect the results? Answer this question also for n = 5,
n = 100 and n = 1000.

## Solution

Code copied from the Week 3.1 R lecture companion...
```{r function-test-hyp-v1}
test.hypothesis.old <- function(significance.level,sample.size,x.sample,probability.hypothesised){
  expected <- sample.size*probability.hypothesised;
  deviation <- abs(x.sample-expected);
  lower.bound <- expected - deviation;
  upper.bound <- expected + deviation;
  upper.bound <- ifelse( (upper.bound-floor(upper.bound)) < .Machine$double.eps, 
                         upper.bound - 1,floor(upper.bound))
  p.value <- 
    pbinom(lower.bound,sample.size,probability.hypothesised) + 
    1 - pbinom(upper.bound,sample.size,probability.hypothesised);
  return(p.value < significance.level);
}
```  
... and modified to answer the questions above...

```{r function-test-hyp}
get.p.value <- function(sample.size, x.sample, probability.hypothesised){
  expected <- sample.size*probability.hypothesised;
  deviation <- abs(x.sample-expected);
  lower.bound <- expected - deviation;
  upper.bound <- expected + deviation;
  upper.bound <- sapply(upper.bound, function(ub) {
    if ((ub-floor(ub)) < .Machine$double.eps) {
      return(ub - 1)
    } else {
      return(floor(ub))
    }
  })

  p.value <- 
    pbinom(lower.bound,sample.size,probability.hypothesised) + 
    1 - pbinom(upper.bound,sample.size,probability.hypothesised);
  return(p.value);
}

test.hypothesis <- function(significance.level,sample.size,x.sample,probability.hypothesised){
  p.value <- get.p.value(sample.size, x.sample,probability.hypothesised);
  return(p.value < significance.level);
}

get.rejected.hypotheses <- function(alpha, sample.size, x, possible.hypothesis) {
  sapply(x,
    function(x.tmp){
      test.hypothesis(alpha, sample.size, x.tmp, possible.hypothesis)
    }
  )
}

```  

```{r}
df <- data.frame()

p.actual <- 0.5
alpha <- 0.05

sample.size.min <- 5
sample.size.max <- 100
sample.size.num.points <- 50
sample.size.values <- 
  floor(seq(sample.size.min, sample.size.max, length.out = sample.size.num.points))

possible.hypothesis.min <- 0
possible.hypothesis.max <- 1
possible.hypothesis.num.points <- 100
possible.hypothesis.values <- 
  seq(possible.hypothesis.min, possible.hypothesis.max, length.out = possible.hypothesis.num.points)

for (sample.size in sample.size.values) {
    x <- rbinom(1, sample.size, p.actual)
    rejected.hypotheses <- get.rejected.hypotheses(alpha, sample.size, x, possible.hypothesis.values)
    df <- rbind(df, data.frame(possible.hypothesis.values, rejected.hypotheses, sample.size))
}

#df <- df[df$rejected.hypotheses == 0, ]
str(df)

plot(x=df$possible.hypothesis.values,
  y=df$sample.size,
  col=c("blue","red")[df$rejected.hypotheses+1],
  pch=19,
  ylab="Sample Size",
  xlab="Possible Hypotheses"
)
```

As we increase the sample size, we accept the hypothesis for a narrower range 
of values for p.

Moving on to part (b)...

We want to iterate across a range of values for p and n.

```{r}
df <- data.frame()

alpha <- 0.05
possible.hypothesis <- 0.5;

sample.size.min <- 5
sample.size.max <- 200
sample.size.num.points <- 50
sample.size.values <- 
  floor(seq(sample.size.min, sample.size.max, length.out = sample.size.num.points))

p.actual.min <- 0
p.actual.max <- 1
p.actual.num.points <- 200
p.actual.values <- seq(p.actual.min, p.actual.max, length.out = p.actual.num.points)

for (sample.size in sample.size.values) {
    for (p.actual in p.actual.values) {
        x <- rbinom(1, sample.size, p.actual)
        rejected.hypotheses <- get.rejected.hypotheses(alpha, sample.size, x, possible.hypothesis)
        df <- rbind(df, data.frame(p.actual, rejected.hypotheses, sample.size))
    }
}

plot(x=df$p.actual,
  y=df$sample.size,
  col=c("blue","red")[df$rejected.hypotheses+1],
  pch=19,
  xlab="p.actual",
  ylab="Sample Size"
)
```

For a given hypothesis, as we increase the sample size, we accept the hypothesis
for a narrower range of values for p.

Part (c) is similar to part 2, but we iterate across a range of values for 
p.hypothesised.

Part(f) is very interesting...

For confidence intervals with fixed n = 10 and p = 0.2, how do the changes of
the confidence level 1 - $\alpha$ affect the results? Answer this question also for n = 5,
n = 100 and n = 1000.

```{r}

sample.size.min <- 50
sample.size.max <- 1000
sample.size.num.points <- 20
sample.size.values <- seq(sample.size.min, sample.size.max, length.out = sample.size.num.points)

p.actual.min <- 0.01
p.actual.max <- 0.5
p.actual.num.points <- 300
p.actual.values <- seq(p.actual.min, p.actual.max, length.out = p.actual.num.points)

alpha.min <- 0.01
alpha.max <- 0.5
alpha.num.points <- 5
alpha.values <- seq(alpha.min, alpha.max, length.out = alpha.num.points)

df <- data.frame()
possible.hypothesis <- 0.5;
for (sample.size in sample.size.values) {
    for (p.actual in p.actual.values) {
        x <- rbinom(1, sample.size, p.actual)
        for (alpha in alpha.values) {
          rejected.hypotheses <- get.rejected.hypotheses(alpha, sample.size, x, possible.hypothesis)
          df <- rbind(df, data.frame(p.actual, rejected.hypotheses, alpha, sample.size))
        }
    }
}
```

```{r}
library(plotly)

# I want to remove all rows where rejected.hypotheses is 0
df <- df[df$rejected.hypotheses == 0, ]

plot_ly(
  data = df,
  x = ~p.actual,
  y = ~alpha,
  z = ~sample.size,
  type = "scatter3d",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~alpha,
  text = ~paste(
    "p.actual:", p.actual,
    "<br>sample.size:", sample.size,
    "<br>alpha:", alpha,
    "<br>Rejected:", rejected.hypotheses
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text",
  marker = list(size = 4)
  #color_continuous_scale=plot_ly.express.colors.sequential.Rainbow
) %>%
  layout(
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "p.actual"),
      yaxis = list(title = "alpha"),
      zaxis = list(title = "sample.size")
    )
  )
```


# Exercise 2

The manufacturer claims that the median lifetime of a component is 25
hours (that means that the lifetime of such a component is equally likely to be below
and above 25 hours). To verify this claim, an analyst decided to select a random sample
of 20 such components, observe their lifetime and count X, the number of observations
exceeding 25 hours.

The sample turned out to contain 8 components with lifetime exceeding 25 hours.
Test a suitable hypothesis and state your conclusion.

# Exercise 6

In a company with 48 male and 41 female employees, the HR department
annually conducts a focus group to discuss the workplace culture. The policy says that
5 employees should be selected fairly and randomly for the focus group.
(a) What probability distribution is appropriate for modelling the number of female
members in the focus group? Calculate the probability that female members are a
majority in the focus group.
(b) A whistleblower reports that female employees were a majority in the focus group
only once in the last 6 years and hence the policy is clearly violated. Conduct an
appropriate statistical analysis and conclude whether the whistleblower's concerns
are valid.

# Exercise 7

Messages consisting of 0s and 1s are transmitted through a noisy channel,
where each bit (binary digit) is either transmitted correctly or flipped (that is, 0 is replaced
by 1 or vice versa). The probability of correct transmission is 0.75 for each transmitted
bit, independently of any other transmitted bits.
For error correction, each bit of the original message is transmitted as a block where
the original bit is repeated 2N + 1 times. The most common bit (occurring at least N + 1
times) in the received block is taken as the received bit. If the received bit is different
from the original bit, this is called a transmission error.
(a) What probability distribution is appropriate for modelling the number of correctly
transmitted bits in a block of size 2N + 1?
(b) Calculate the probability of a transmission error for a block of length 5 (that is,
when N = 2).
(c) It is known that 73 transmission errors occurred in a message having the original
length of 512. Using an appropriate statistical procedure, decide whether blocks of
length 5 were used for error correction in that case.
(d) Find the minimal block length 2N + 1 such that the probability of a transmission
error is less than 1%.
